Patient history. A woman aged 31
years with an uneventful family and medical history developed a
slowly progressive stiffness and rigidity in axial muscles 10 years
earlier. She had painful muscle spasms triggered by tactile and
emotional stimuli, partial complex seizures, and paroxysmal auto-
nomic dysfunction with tachycardia, hyperidrosis, and itch at-
tacks. Clinical examination showed hyperlordosis of the lumbar
spine. The muscular tone was markedly increased in the paraspi-
nal region and proximally in the lower limbs. Spontaneous and
touch-sensitive flexor spasms of the arms and legs were present.
Deep tendon reflexes were normal and symmetric with flexor
plantar responses. An EMG showed continuous electric activity at
rest in the thoracoabdominal muscles. SPS was then diagnosed,
and diazepam treatment was started (50 mg/d) with temporary
response. Subsequent progression of the disease to the lower limbs
hampered the gait. After a good response to baclofen treatment,
she became pregnant. All drugs were discontinued with a subse-
quent clinical deterioration.
At the 20th week of pregnancy, a sample of amnion and blood
from the funiculus was taken, and anti-GAD65 was detected in
the amniotic fluid and fetal and maternal serum. At the 39th
week, the newborn was delivered by cesarean section. Clinical and
neurologic examinations of the newborn were normal. A week
after delivery, drugs were successfully started again. Two years
later, the patient entered her second pregnancy, and treatment
was discontinued. Although she worsened, she delivered a second
healthy newborn at the 40th week.

High titer of anti-GAD65 was evident in the two infants until
age 24 months (table), but no signs of SPS or other anti-GAD-
related diseases were detected at 6- and 8-year follow-up
evaluations.

Results. The profile of anti-GAD65 in the mother and
two newborns is summarized in the table. Sera from 86
blood donors were negative in all assays.
